subject: Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density

messages.author: 0c5c0e757cf4ae54
messages.subject: Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density
parts:
Hi all,

I am a new user to STAN and am having problems probably with initial values but I still do not know to fix it.
I attached the data, full Rstan code, the error log and the R session info in this email.

Any comments would be highly appreciated.
Best regards,
Teo


Below is part of the error and the code for a quick look.

==== Part of error log ====
Error in function stan::prob::lognormal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable is -0.327444:0, but must be >= 0!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
=====================


==== STAN code ====
data {

  int<lower=0> J;
  int<lower=0> J2;
  int<lower=0> margin;
  real Ytau;
  real y[J]; 
  real x1[J];
  real x2[J];
  real x3[J];
  real z1[J];
  real z2[J];
  real z3[J];

}

parameters {

  real omega;
  real alpha0;
  real sigma0;
  real sigma1;
  real sigma2;
  real sigma3;
  real srho1;
  real srho2;
  real srho3;
  real<lower=0> gamma1;
  real<lower=0> gamma2;
  real<lower=0> gamma3;
  real<lower=0> beta1[J2];
  real<lower=0> beta2[J2];
  real<lower=0> beta3[J2];
  real dalpha[J2];

}

transformed parameters {
  
  real mu[J2];
  real alpha[J2];
  real rho1;
  real rho2;
  real rho3;
  real S1[J];
  real S2[J];
  real S3[J];
  
  alpha[1] <- alpha0;
  
  rho1 <- inv_logit(-srho1);
  rho2 <- inv_logit(-srho2);
  rho3 <- inv_logit(-srho3);
  
  S1[1] <- x1[1];
  S2[1] <- x2[1];
  S3[1] <- x3[1];
  
  for(s in 1:J-1){
    S1[s+1] <- rho1*S1[s] + x1[s+1];
    S2[s+1] <- rho2*S2[s] + x2[s+1];
    S3[s+1] <- rho3*S3[s] + x3[s+1];
  }
  
  for(t in 2:J-margin) {
    alpha[t] <- dalpha[t]*alpha[t-1];
  }
  
  for(t in 1:J-margin){
    mu[t] <- alpha[t] + beta1[t]*S1[margin+t] + beta2[t]*S2[margin+t] + beta3[t]*S3[margin+t] 
           + gamma1*z1[margin+t] - gamma2*z2[margin+t] - gamma3*z3[margin+t];
  }

}

model{

  omega ~ gamma(2,2);
  alpha0 ~ gamma(100,Ytau);
  sigma0 ~ gamma(2,20); 
  sigma1 ~ gamma(2,20); 
  sigma2 ~ gamma(2,20); 
  sigma3 ~ gamma(2,20); 
  
  dalpha[1] ~ lognormal(0,1);
  beta1[1] ~ lognormal(0,1);
  beta2[1] ~ lognormal(0,1);
  beta2[1] ~ lognormal(0,1);
  srho1 ~ normal(0,1);
  srho2 ~ normal(0,1);
  srho3 ~ normal(0,1);
  gamma1 ~ lognormal(0,1);
  gamma2 ~ lognormal(0,1);
  gamma3 ~ lognormal(0,1);
  
  for(t in 2:J-margin){                                                            
    dalpha[t] ~ lognormal(log(dalpha[t-1]),sigma0);
    beta1[t] ~ lognormal(log(beta1[t-1]),sigma1);
    beta2[t] ~ lognormal(log(beta2[t-1]),sigma2);
    beta3[t] ~ lognormal(log(beta3[t-1]),sigma3);
  }
  
  for(t in 1:J-margin) {
    y[margin+t] ~ normal(mu[t],omega);
  }

}
========================

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density
parts:
The parameters need to be declared with constraints
that match their support in the model (technically, it's
only a one-way requirement --- parameters that meet the
constraints should have non-zero density).

In particular, you need to declare all the variables
modeled with gamma or lognormal distributions with
constraint <lower=0>. This includes most of your parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density
parts:
You want to measure effective samples per second, not
iteration time. And 10,000 samples is likely to be far
more than you need for most applications --- look at your
MCMC standard error, which is what goes down as 1/sqrt(n_eff).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density
parts: You can also speed the program up by vectorizing all of these:

> for(t in 2:J-margin){
> > dalpha[t] ~ lognormal(log(dalpha[t-1]),sigma0);
> > beta1[t] ~ lognormal(log(beta1[t-1]),sigma1);
> > beta2[t] ~ lognormal(log(beta2[t-1]),sigma2);
> > beta3[t] ~ lognormal(log(beta3[t-1]),sigma3);
> > }
> >
> > for(t in 1:J-margin) {
> > y[margin+t] ~ normal(mu[t],omega);
> > }

using vector slicing. For example, the top loop can be replaced
by replacing each statement inside the loop with something like this:

segment(dalpha,2,J-margin-1) ~ lognormal(segment(dalpha,1,J-margin-2), sigma0);

It will be a lot faster. And apply the log around segment() if that's
what you wanted. You will have to redeclare dalpha as vector[J2] dalpha.
Also, unless J-margin = J2, you'll be missing elements in the sampling.

Also, are you sure you want that log in the lognormal mean? The
parameter mu in y ~ lognormal(mu,sigma) is the mean of log(y),
not the mean of y. We should put that in words, not just leave it implicit
in the formula.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density
parts:
Hi Bob,

Thank you for your insights.

>You want to measure effective samples per second, not
>iteration time.  And 10,000 samples is likely to be far
>more than you need for most applications --- look at your
>MCMC standard error, which is what goes down as 1/sqrt(n_eff).

I still do not know how to use the information on n_eff.
Should I compare the n_eff (or MCMC standart error) between parameters or between simulation runs?
I am sorry that I am new to MCMC and STAN. I will read more on the manual.

segment(dalpha,2,J-margin-1) ~ lognormal(segment(dalpha,1,J-margin-2), sigma0);

It will be a lot faster.  And apply the log around segment() if that's
what you wanted.  You will have to redeclare dalpha as vector[J2] dalpha.
Also, unless J-margin = J2, you'll be missing elements in the sampling.

Yes, the program runs faster when applying vector slicing.
Also it is true that J-margin=J2.
Your sample code did not work due to a subtle miss on index, I think,  
but I fixed as below and it ran well.

   segment(dalpha,2,J-margin-1) ~ lognormal(log(segment(dalpha,1,J-margin-1)), sigma0);

Also, are you sure you want that log in the lognormal mean?  The
parameter mu in y ~ lognormal(mu,sigma) is the mean of log(y),
not the mean of y.  We should put that in words, not just leave it implicit
in the formula.

Yes, I want that log in the lognormal mean since the sampling I want to do is this.
      log(dalpha[t]) ~ normal(log(dalpha[t-1]), sigma0)

- Teo

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error: Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density
parts:
The mcmc standard error (the equivalent of usual standard
error for i.i.d. samples) is given by sd / sqrt(n_eff), where
sd is the posterior standard deviation and n_eff the number of
effective samples. So it determines how tightly your posterior means
(or other derived expectations) are estimated. So it's what you
care about in determining speed --- how long does it take to get
to the desired level of MCMC std error?

And thanks for the clarification on lognormal --- our parameterization
confuses me because we have y and mu on different scales (y is on linear
scale and mu on the log scale).

- Bob

Hi Bob,

Now I am clear with the mcmc standard error.
I will also conduct a fairer comparison with rjags.

Thanks for your support.

- Teo

On Sat, Sep 6, 2014 at 1:12 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
The mcmc standard error (the equivalent of usual standard
error for i.i.d. samples) is given by sd / sqrt(n_eff), where
sd is the posterior standard deviation and n_eff the number of
effective samples.  So it determines how tightly your posterior means
(or other derived expectations) are estimated.  So it's what you
care about in determining speed --- how long does it take to get
to the desired level of MCMC std error?

And thanks for the clarification on lognormal --- our parameterization
confuses me because we have y and mu on different scales (y is on linear
scale and mu on the log scale).

- Bob


On Sep 4, 2014, at 11:02 PM, Teo Nguyen <nguyen...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Bob,
>
> Thank you for your insights.
>
> >You want to measure effective samples per second, not
> >iteration time.  And 10,000 samples is likely to be far
> >more than you need for most applications --- look at your
> >MCMC standard error, which is what goes down as 1/sqrt(n_eff).
>
> I still do not know how to use the information on n_eff.
> Should I compare the n_eff (or MCMC standart error) between parameters or between simulation runs?
> I am sorry that I am new to MCMC and STAN. I will read more on the manual.
>
>    segment(dalpha,2,J-margin-1) ~ lognormal(segment(dalpha,1,J-margin-2), sigma0);
>
> It will be a lot faster.  And apply the log around segment() if that's
> what you wanted.  You will have to redeclare dalpha as vector[J2] dalpha.
> Also, unless J-margin = J2, you'll be missing elements in the sampling.
>
> Yes, the program runs faster when applying vector slicing.
> Also it is true that J-margin=J2.
> Your sample code did not work due to a subtle miss on index, I think,
> but I fixed as below and it ran well.
>
>    segment(dalpha,2,J-margin-1) ~ lognormal(log(segment(dalpha,1,J-margin-1)), sigma0);
>
> Also, are you sure you want that log in the lognormal mean?  The
> parameter mu in y ~ lognormal(mu,sigma) is the mean of log(y),
> not the mean of y.  We should put that in words, not just leave it implicit
> in the formula.
>
> Yes, I want that log in the lognormal mean since the sampling I want to do is this.
>       log(dalpha[t]) ~ normal(log(dalpha[t-1]), sigma0)
>
> - Teo
>
>
>
> - Bob

> > Hi Bob,

> > while a same model written in "rjags" finished in less than 2 minutes.

> > Teo

> > constraints should have non-zero density).
> >
> > In particular, you need to declare all the variables
> > modeled with gamma or lognormal distributions with
